claims.text: The initial alloy is a near-equiatomic FCC Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy.
Rapid quenching produces a baseline with minimal short-range chemical order.
Rapid quenching produces a baseline with limited elemental clustering.
Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys can develop increased unlike-pair chemical ordering.
Annealing at 800–900 K for 1–24 hours followed by slow cooling will enhance SRO relative to a rapidly quenched baseline.
Enhanced SRO will form nanoscale, coherent, chemically ordered clusters within the FCC matrix.
Enhanced SRO lowers the free energy of the FCC solid solution.
Lowering the FCC solid-solution free energy stabilizes the alloy against transformation to secondary phases.
Enhanced SRO suppresses nucleation of deleterious secondary phases.
Local chemical ordering modulates dislocation mobility.
Local chemical ordering increases defect-sink efficiency.
Increased defect-sink efficiency reduces irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Annealed alloys with enhanced SRO will have higher elevated-temperature hardness and strength than the rapidly quenched baseline.
Annealed alloys with enhanced SRO will exhibit less irradiation-induced swelling and defect formation than the baseline.
Annealed alloys with enhanced SRO will have improved oxidation or environmental resistance because their microstructure is more stable.
Annealed alloys with enhanced SRO will have greater cryogenic toughness than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The proposed comparison holds alloy composition and subsequent test conditions constant while varying thermal history.
The hypothesis is restricted to near-equiatomic FCC Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni treated at 800–900 K for 1–24 hours, provided grain coarsening and unwanted precipitation are absent or controlled.
